intent: Public API endpoints get a token-bucket rate limiter keyed by API key, returning 429 with Retry-After once a client exceeds its budget.

story.label: Goal
story.text: Protect the public API from a single client exhausting the service: per-key rate limiting with a token bucket, off by default in development.

story.link: a limiter needs a decision point on the request path — that is a middleware in this codebase

story.label: Step 1 · middleware
story.text: New rateLimit middleware on the /api/* route group: refills the bucket from elapsed time, takes a token, sets X-RateLimit-Remaining. Two outcomes:
branches: request passes through, remaining tokens reported in the response headers
429 with Retry-After; the body follows the project-wide error shape from errorHandler

story.link: counters must stay correct across instances — a naive GET+SET loses increments under concurrent load

story.label: Consequence · Redis
story.text: Bucket state is an INCR-and-EXPIRE pair executed as one atomic Lua script; keys are rl:{key}:{window} with a TTL, so state cleans itself up.

story.link: limits differ per environment, so they come from config rather than constants

story.label: Consequence · config
story.text: Two new env vars: RATE_LIMIT_RPM (requests per minute) and RATE_LIMIT_BURST. Unset RPM disables the limiter — development stays friction-free, and the rollout is a config change.

story.label: Confirmation
story.text: 12 tests: refill math including burst, both middleware outcomes, per-key isolation, the 429 response shape, and the limiter staying off when RPM is unset.

groups.name: Decision record
groups.why: Fixes the scope decisions: token bucket over sliding window (cheaper, burst-friendly), fail-open when Redis is down (availability over strictness for a public API), health checks and webhooks stay outside the limiter.

groups.name: Core: token bucket and the 429 path
groups.why: The middleware is the decision point: refill math, key derivation (API key, IP fallback), and the throttled response. Two things worth checking by hand: the refill formula under burst, and that the 429 body reuses the shared error shape instead of inventing its own.

groups.name: Redis: atomic counters
groups.why: One new helper, one pattern to verify: the INCR+EXPIRE pair must be a single atomic script, and every key must carry a TTL — a keyless EXPIRE or a two-step counter reintroduces the race this exists to close.

groups.name: Config & rollout
groups.why: The limiter ships dark: with RATE_LIMIT_RPM unset nothing changes. Turning it on is a config-only rollout, and turning it off again is deleting one env var.

groups.name: Behavior fixed by tests
groups.why: 12 tests pin the refill math (including burst), both middleware outcomes, per-key isolation, the 429 shape with Retry-After, and the disabled-by-default behavior.

docs/rate-limiting.md.why: Key decisions: token bucket over sliding window (constant memory, burst-friendly); fail-open when Redis is unavailable — for a public API, availability wins over strict limiting; health checks and webhooks deliberately stay outside /api/* scope.
frag: - Token bucket, not sliding window: constant memory, allows bursts.
- Fail-open on Redis outage: availability over strictness.
- Health checks and webhooks are not throttled (outside /api/*).

src/middleware/rateLimit.ts.why: What happened: the middleware derives the bucket key (API key, IP fallback), refills tokens from elapsed time, and either passes the request through with X-RateLimit-Remaining or throws a 429. Review focus: the refill formula caps at burst size — check the rounding; and the 429 goes through the shared ApiError, not a hand-rolled response.

src/routes/api.ts.why: What happened: the limiter is mounted on the /api/* router group, after auth (so the key is known) and before handlers. Health and webhook routes live outside the group and stay unthrottled.

src/middleware/errorHandler.ts.why: What happened: the shared error handler learns the 429 case: it keeps Retry-After set by the limiter and renders the standard { code, message } body, so clients parse one error shape everywhere.
frag: // Retry-After is already on the response when the limiter threw.
return res.status(err.status).json({ code: err.code, message: err.message });
preview: 429 renders the standard { code, message } body

src/lib/redis.ts.why: What happened: takeToken runs INCR and EXPIRE as one Lua script — the counter and its TTL can never diverge, and concurrent requests cannot lose increments. Review focus: the script is the whole point; a JS-side two-step would silently reintroduce the race.
frag: if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
preview: INCR + EXPIRE as one Lua script (atomic)

src/config.ts.why: What happened: rateLimit config block: RATE_LIMIT_RPM and RATE_LIMIT_BURST, both optional. Unset RPM yields enabled: false — the middleware becomes a no-op, which is also the rollback path.

test/rateLimit.test.ts.why: What happened: fake clock plus in-memory Redis stub; covers refill math (burst cap, partial refill), both middleware outcomes, per-key isolation (one client cannot drain another's bucket), the 429 shape with Retry-After, and the limiter staying off when RPM is unset.

test('throttled request → 429, Retry-After, standard error body')
test('keys are isolated: client A cannot exhaust client B')
test('RATE_LIMIT_RPM unset → middleware is a no-op')

standards.finding: The 60-second window is a literal inside the middleware while every other limit comes from config. A second call site (e.g. a per-route override) would silently disagree with it.
standards.pattern: config-first: all tunables live in src/config.ts

standards.finding: takeToken returns the raw counter and the middleware derives tokens from it; an explicit { remaining, retryAfter } return would read better, but this matches the thin-helper style of src/lib.
Project conventions hold: middleware pattern for cross-cutting concerns, shared ApiError shape, config-driven behavior with a safe default (off).

tests.summary: 12 tests in one new file. The bucket math and both middleware outcomes are pinned; what is NOT covered is concurrency against a real Redis and the fail-open path.
fixed: Refill math: partial refill over elapsed time, capped at RATE_LIMIT_BURST
Throttled request → 429 with Retry-After and the standard { code, message } body
Per-key isolation: one client cannot drain another client's bucket
IP fallback is used when no API key header is present
RATE_LIMIT_RPM unset → middleware is a no-op (rollout/rollback path)
gaps: Concurrency against a real Redis (tests use an in-memory stub; the Lua atomicity itself is unverified)
Fail-open when Redis is down — the decision exists in docs, not in a test
Retry-After correctness across a window boundary (clock skew)

env.name: RATE_LIMIT_RPM
env.note: requests per minute per key; unset = limiter off

deploy: Ships dark: deploy first, then set RATE_LIMIT_RPM to enable — rollback is deleting the var
Redis 6.2+ required (Lua script uses INCR/EXPIRE semantics verified there)
ops.note: No migrations — counters are ephemeral Redis keys with a TTL; nothing persistent changes shape.

blastRadius.why: Lives outside /api/* and stays unthrottled — verify that is intended, or a noisy webhook sender can still exhaust the service.
The proxy already has a coarse limit_req zone; two layers can double-throttle bursts near the limit.
Runs before the limiter, so unauthenticated floods hit auth (and its DB lookups) unthrottled — the limiter only protects what is behind it.
